newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Mexico finalize tomato agreement.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico finalize tomato agreement.

text.p: The U.S. government and Mexican tomato growers finalised an agreement this week that officially settles a bitter bilateral trade dispute over the alleged dumping of Mexican produce in the United States, the Commerce Department said Tuesday.
The agreement, reached earlier this month and signed on Monday, sets a floor price of about $5.17 per 25-pound box for Mexican tomatoes sold in the United States.

Florida tomato growers filed a trade complaint last spring against Mexican growers, charging that Mexico was unfairly selling its tomatoes in American markets at below-market prices and costing the Florida industry hundreds of millions of dollars in lost sales.
This past winter, wholesale tomato prices dropped to as low as $3 per box because of increased supplies and competition.

"The agreement is very beneficial to tomato growers in Florida and other states, and it will help preserve jobs in the industry," Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said in an agency announcement on the pact.

Critics of the Florida complaint have contended that Florida growers were seeking undue protection in an election year, and that because of Florida's 25 electoral votes, the Clinton administration has looked more sympathetically at the U.S. industry's complaint.

Just prior to signing the so-called suspension agreement, the Commerce Department issued a preliminary finding that Mexican tomatoes were being sold in the United States at an average of 17.56 percent below the market price. If the suspension agreement had not been negotiated, Mexican tomatoes might have been subject to an import duty of 17.56 percent.

In a related development Tuesday, the Agriculture Department proposed exempting some Florida growers from certain weight requirements. The exemption, according to industry officials, would favour the packing of more vine-ripe tomatoes and make Florida tomatoes more competitive with Mexican-grown produce.
Mexico generally ships vine-ripened tomatoes, while Florida growers commonly pick their tomatoes green and then artificially ripen them. Many consumers say vine-ripened tomatoes are tastier.
The proposed exemption, if approved, would go into effect by this winter, the peak marketing time for Florida tomatoes.
